explanations.explanation: Burned is it. The text says the Amalekites "had raided the Negev, attacked Ziklag, and burned it down." That's a whole town gone, and I once scorched a single batch and felt terrible. David's men come home to this, friend, so I'll keep my burnt cookie complaints to myself.

Tore sounds like a natural word for a raid, but it isn't the one in the text. The verse says the Amalekites "attacked Ziklag, and burned it down." So it wasn't pulled apart. It was set on fire, and that's a very different kind of cleanup.
Knocked it down is a good guess, friend, because raids can do that. But the text uses a different word. The Amalekites "attacked Ziklag, and burned it down." Fire is what finished the town.

I get why that sounds right after a raid like this, but hold on. Verse 2 says, "They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way." The women and everyone else, young and old, were taken captive. That's still a terrible day, and I think it's also why David has a reason to hope.

False is right, friend. The text says, "They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way." The people were taken captive, both young and old. That matters, because captives can still be found.

explanations.answer: Weep until they have no strength left
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. David and his troops "lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep." These are soldiers, friend, and they cry until there's nothing left. I think that part is just plain heartbreaking, and I'm not going to joke about it.

explanations.answer: Sit in silence for seven days
explanations.explanation: There's no silence in this verse, friend. It's loud. David and the troops "lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep." And no seven days are mentioned here at all.

explanations.answer: Chase the raiders that same hour
explanations.explanation: I love the energy, but the chase comes later. The first thing the text shows is that David and his troops "lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep." Sometimes the first thing that happens is crying, and the text doesn't rush past it. David doesn't head out until he's asked the LORD about it.

Abigail it is, the widow of Nabal of Carmel. The text names David's two captive wives as Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail. These two aren't just names on a list, friend. They're the people David is about to go after.

Michal is a fair guess, since she was David's wife too. Saul, Israel's king, gave her to him as a wife (1 Samuel 18:27). But this verse names the two captives as Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel. Abigail is the one that fills the blank.

Merab is a name from David's earlier story, friend. She was Saul's older daughter, offered to David but then given to someone else (1 Samuel 18:17, 19). She isn't named here. This verse says Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel, were taken captive.

Yes. The text says David was greatly distressed "because the people spoke of stoning him." These are men who just lost their sons and daughters, and they aim all that pain at their leader. I think David is hurting plenty on his own, and now his own people are muttering about stones.

That's a reasonable guess for a camp in turmoil, but it's not in the text. The verse says David was greatly distressed "because the people spoke of stoning him." It's much more serious than a leadership vote, friend. The text also says the soul of every man grieved for his sons and daughters.

Nobody mentions the Philistine army in this verse, friend. What the text says is that David was greatly distressed "because the people spoke of stoning him." The men are hurting over their sons and daughters, and that's what the talk is about. I think it must have been a long, awful night in that camp.

That's the one. "But David found strength in the LORD his God." Look at the timing, friend. His town is burned, his family is gone, and his own men are talking about stoning him, and the text says he finds his strength in the LORD.

That's a nice thought, but look at the verse. His men are the ones talking about stoning him. The text says, "But David found strength in the LORD his God." Sometimes the people next to you are hurting too much to hold you up.

David doesn't have a plan yet at this point, friend. The text says, "But David found strength in the LORD his God." The strength comes first, and then he asks the LORD what to do. I'd say that's the right order.
True, friend. David tells Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, to bring the ephod. Then "David inquired of the LORD." He asks before he does anything else.
It's true, friend. The text says Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, brought the ephod, and then "David inquired of the LORD." He doesn't skip that step. He asks before he moves.

explanations.answer: Pursue and you will rescue the captives
explanations.explanation: That's it. David asks, "Should I pursue these raiders? Will I overtake them?" and the LORD answers, "Pursue them, for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives." David asks two questions and gets a full yes to both. When the LORD tells you to go, friend, you can go.

explanations.answer: Stay and rebuild your town first
explanations.explanation: That sounds sensible, but it's not what the LORD says. David asks if he should pursue the raiders and if he'll overtake them. The LORD answers, "Pursue them, for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives." The town can wait, because the captives can't.

explanations.answer: Wait here and they will come back
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't tell David to wait. His answer is, "Pursue them, for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives." It's a go, friend, and David hears it clearly. Nobody is told to sit tight and hope.

Two hundred is right. The text says "two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook." That leaves David with four hundred to keep going. Run all night after that kind of heartbreak and I think your legs would quit too.
Close, but it's more than that. The text says "two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook." That's a third of the six hundred. David continues on with four hundred.

Three hundred would be half the group, friend, and that's too many. The text says "two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook." David "and four hundred men continued in pursuit." Six hundred minus two hundred leaves four hundred.

Not quite. The text says two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook, "But David and four hundred men continued in pursuit." He doesn't stop and wait for them. The two hundred stay behind, and the chase keeps going.
False is right. Two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook, "But David and four hundred men continued in pursuit." He keeps moving. The two hundred stay behind at the Brook of Besor.

I can see why you'd think that, but the text goes another way. David's men find the Egyptian in the field and bring him to David. Then "They gave the man water to drink and food to eat." Nobody's tied up. He gets a meal.

False is right, friend. The text says David's men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. Then "They gave the man water to drink and food to eat." Nothing in the verse says anyone tied him up.

Three days and three nights is right. The text says "he had not had any food or water for three days and three nights." Then he gets a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins, and he's revived. After that long, I think a fig cake would taste like the finest thing in the world.

It was longer than that, friend. The text says he "had not had any food or water for three days and three nights." That's why a little fig cake and some raisins revive him. One day would be rough, but three days and three nights is a lot worse.

That's more than the text says. It reads, "he had not had any food or water for three days and three nights." The man's master abandoned him when he fell ill. That's the whole stretch he'd gone without.
An Amalekite, yes. The man says, "I am an Egyptian... the slave of an Amalekite." That's the same people who raided Ziklag. So David is talking to someone who knows exactly where the raiders went.

A Philistine would make some sense in this story, friend, but it's not what he says. His words are, "I am an Egyptian... the slave of an Amalekite." The Amalekites are the raiders, so he's tied to them. That's why David's question matters so much.

Moabite isn't in this scene at all, friend. The man tells David, "I am an Egyptian... the slave of an Amalekite." His master belongs to the raiding party. That detail turns out to be the key to the whole chase.
It's not true, friend. The Egyptian says, "My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill." He didn't run off. He got sick and was left behind. Nothing in his words says he tried to escape.

False is right. The man says, "My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill." It was illness, and nothing about escaping. I think that's a sad way to be treated, and it leaves him wanting help.

explanations.answer: Not to kill him or hand him over
explanations.explanation: That's it. He says, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master, and I will lead you to them." He's already been left behind once, so I think he wants a promise before he trusts anyone. In return he'll lead David right to the raiders.

explanations.answer: To give him a share of the plunder
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, but plunder isn't what he asks for. He says, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master, and I will lead you to them." He wants to be safe. That's the whole deal.

explanations.answer: To send him safely home to Egypt
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice ending for him, but it's not what he asks. He says, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master, and I will lead you to them." He asks not to be killed and not to be handed back to his master.

Yes. The Amalekites were "eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah." They're spread out and having a party. It's a lot of loot and a lot of confidence.

Nobody's asleep in this verse, friend. The text says the Amalekites were "eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder." They're awake and having a party. It's a big spread, and they're enjoying it.

They're not packing, friend. They're "spread out over all the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken." They look like they're settling in for a good time. That's what David finds when the Egyptian leads him there.
Almost, but the text has an exception. David struck them down, "Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels." So some got away, and they got away fast.
False is right. The text says, "Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels." Four hundred got away. It's a big fight, and it still has that one exception.

All of it, friend. "David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives." The text adds, "Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken." Every person and every bit of plunder came back.

The people did come back, and that's the best part. But the text goes further: "Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken. David brought everything back." That means the plunder too.

Livestock is part of it, but it isn't the whole story. The text says, "David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives." It also says, "Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter." The people came home, and I think that's what mattered most.

explanations.answer: Give them only their wives and children
explanations.explanation: That's the plan. Those men say, "Because they did not go with us, we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man's wife and children. They may take them and go." The text calls them "wicked and worthless men." They want to cut the exhausted ones out of the plunder completely.

explanations.answer: Make them carry all the plunder home
explanations.explanation: Nobody says anything about carrying in the text. What the men say is, "we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man's wife and children. They may take them and go." So the plan is to hold back the plunder. The two hundred are only allowed to take their families.

explanations.answer: Send them back to the Philistine army
explanations.explanation: The Philistine army isn't part of this plan, friend. The men say, "we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man's wife and children. They may take them and go." That's all they say. They just want to keep the plunder to themselves.

explanations.answer: The LORD gave it and protected them
explanations.explanation: That's his reason. David says, "you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us." So the plunder is a gift from the LORD, and it isn't something to hoard. David puts the credit where it belongs.

explanations.answer: The two hundred are his own family
explanations.explanation: David does call them "My brothers," but he doesn't say they're his family. The reason he gives is, "you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us." It's about what the LORD gave.

explanations.answer: Saul would punish them for it
explanations.explanation: Saul never comes up in David's answer, friend. David says, "you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us." His reason is that the LORD gave it and the LORD protected them.

Match is the word. David says, "The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike." Same share for both, friend. Whoever watched the supplies gets the same as whoever fought.
Double isn't what he says. David says the share of the one who went to battle "will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies." He adds, "They will share alike." It's an even split.

Triple would be a big bonus for the fighters, friend, but David doesn't go for that. His ruling is that the share of the one who went to battle "will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike." Equal shares for both.

True, friend. The text says, "And so it has been from that day forward. David established this statute and ordinance for Israel to this very day." That one ruling at the Brook of Besor lasted a long time.

It's true, friend. The text says, "And so it has been from that day forward. David established this statute and ordinance for Israel to this very day." His ruling at the Brook of Besor became a lasting rule. I think that's one worth keeping.

Elders is right. David sends it to "his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, 'Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD's enemies.'" He calls them his friends. He shares what he has, and I think that's a good way to be.

Priests aren't the ones named here, friend. The text says David sent the gift to "his friends, the elders of Judah." He calls the plunder "the plunder of the LORD's enemies." So it's the elders who get the gifts.

Captains is a decent guess for a man who just won a battle, but the text says something else. David sends the gifts to "his friends, the elders of Judah." His message is, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD's enemies." So the blank is elders.
